title: Factor-two graph distances in logarithmically many passes
formal:
Can a randomized streaming algorithm estimate the distance between two specified vertices of an undirected, unweighted graph within a factor of two using \(O(\log n)\) passes and \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) bits of memory?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that the following holds for every simple graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every specified pair \(s,t\), and every ordering of its edges? The algorithm knows \(n,s,t\) before the stream begins, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\text{ passes},\]
and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs \(D\) satisfying
\[d_G(s,t)\le D\le2d_G(s,t).\]
For disconnected \(s,t\), success means outputting the symbol \(\infty\). All passes read the same edge order.
why: Shortest-path distance is a basic graph quantity whose global dependencies challenge small-memory sequential access. This question isolates the number of scans needed for a useful constant-factor estimate, between new near-logarithmic lower bounds and the best verified upper bounds.
status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 14, Kanpur 2006, updated 25 September 2016. The user selected factor-two single-pair estimation in O(log n) passes and O(n polylog n) bits. The SODA 2026 publication of Assadi–Hoppenworth–Sundaresan and its 21 October 2025 full version were checked on 16 September 2026. Their constant-factor upper bound uses O((log n/log log n)^2) passes; their lower bound is Omega(log n/log log n), including fixed-pair unweighted instances and a same-order simulation. These statements leave the selected target unresolved. A bounded later-work search found no verified closure of this gap. No new algorithm, lower-bound proof or Lean formalization is claimed.

progress.text: Problem 14 explicitly asks for distance approximation in logarithmically many passes and records a then-known distance-threshold lower bound.

Assadi, Hoppenworth and Sundaresan publish upper and lower pass bounds leaving a gap between \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) and \(O((\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) for constant-factor approximation in semi-streaming space. Neither bound settles the chosen \(O(\log n)\) target.

importance.reason: A longstanding core graph-streaming problem with a sharply stated resource target inside a recently narrowed upper/lower bound gap. It tests the limits of repeated sequential access even for minimal single-pair output.

sentences: The problem asks for a factor-two estimate of one specified distance in an undirected unweighted graph stream.
The source and target are known in advance, and every pass sees the same arbitrary edge order.
The algorithm may use n times a fixed polylogarithmic number of bits but only logarithmically many passes.
Published 2026 bounds leave this target between a near-logarithmic lower bound and a larger upper bound.
A resolution would clarify how repeated sequential access recovers global graph distances with limited memory.

definitions:
The input graph is finite, undirected, unweighted and simple: there are no self-loops or parallel edges. Its vertices have distinct binary labels in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\). Each edge appears exactly once as an unordered pair of labels. The stream lists these edges explicitly in an arbitrary order, with an end marker; it may be empty. Isolated vertices are included in the known vertex set even though they do not appear in any edge. No planarity, sparsity, degree or diameter restriction is imposed.

The vertices \(s,t\) belong to the known vertex set and are supplied before any edge is read. They may be equal. A path has length equal to its number of edges, and \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(s\) to \(t\). Set \(d_G(s,s)=0\) and \(d_G(s,t)=\infty\) if there is no connecting path. Every finite distance is an integer between zero and \(n-1\).

A pass scans the edge list once from beginning to end. After a pass the algorithm may rewind to the beginning and retain its memory, but it cannot reorder or change the stream. Within a pass it has only sequential access. There is no random access to old edges, adjacency-query oracle, external scratch file or separate stored copy of the graph. All passes encounter the same fixed order. The algorithm may stop after fewer passes than its bound; starting another scan counts as another pass.

The output is one integer \(D\) or the distinguished symbol \(\infty\). The algorithm need not output a path, a spanning tree, distances to other targets or a summary supporting later queries. Integer output loses no generality for this factor guarantee: rounding down a nonnegative real estimate in the permitted interval preserves both inequalities when the true distance is an integer. For a connected pair the successful output lies between \(d_G(s,t)\) and \(2d_G(s,t)\), with no additive error. For a disconnected pair the successful output is \(\infty\); for \(s=t\) it is zero.

For every fixed graph, edge ordering and pair, probability is over the algorithm's independent fair random bits. The input and its order are fixed independently of those bits. The success condition concerns the single requested output. It is not an average over graphs or stream orders, and it does not require one random seed to work for all inputs simultaneously.

Use one finite uniform program for every input size. Its memory consists of all mutable working information, including retained edge data, vertex labels, counters, stored random choices and output preparation. Every bit of that information counts. Fresh random bits may be read as needed, but old random bits cannot be revisited unless their information was retained within the space bound. The graph stream is read-only external input. The supplied parameters take only \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, so charging their storage does not change the target.

Both resource bounds hold throughout every execution, including unsuccessful random executions. The algorithm must halt and produce an output; no bound on local computation time is imposed beyond this termination requirement. Thus the question isolates memory and passes, as in the streaming source. Computationally expensive processing between edges cannot hide extra memory or reread the input. A polynomial local-time algorithm would suffice, but such a time requirement is not added to the target.

The constants \(C_s,C_p\) and the exponent \(k\) are fixed independently of \(n\), the graph, the stream order, the distance and the random choices. The memory notation \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) permits any fixed power of the logarithm. The pass bound permits only one power: an arbitrary \(O(\log^c n)\) bound for a fixed \(c>1\) is not the requested \(O(\log n)\) result. Binary logarithms with the harmless \(n+2\) offset avoid small-input exceptions.

The term semi-streaming refers to memory proportional to the number of vertices times a fixed power of the logarithm, even though a dense graph can have quadratically many edges. Papers often count \(O(\log n)\)-bit words rather than bits. This changes the permitted logarithmic power by one and therefore describes the same space class here. When a particular logarithmic space bound is quoted, its unit must still be stated.

The selected model is insertion-only and allows every fixed edge ordering. Edge deletions, random-order streams and a source or target revealed only after streaming are separately quantified variants. Likewise, all-pairs distances and single-source shortest-path trees ask for more output than this card. The original source combines several of these questions. With the user's approval, this card retains just factor-two estimation of one known pair in logarithmically many passes.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the algorithm and constants in the statement, including its success probability for every graph and order and its worst-case bit-space and pass bounds. Alternatively, provide a complete Lean-checked proof that no such uniform randomized algorithm exists. The negative direction must rule out every fixed polylogarithmic space exponent \(k\) together with an \(O(\log n)\) pass bound; a lower bound for one narrower space allowance does not suffice. A lower bound of only \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\), or an upper bound with \(O((\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) passes, leaves the selected target unresolved. Improved constants, a larger approximation factor, an additive error, average-order correctness or correctness only for nearby vertices do not settle this exact resource-and-error question.

source_formulation.text: McGregor asks how well the distance between two specified vertices can be estimated from an edge stream, particularly in O(log n) passes, and separately mentions random-order input. The user selected factor two, undirected unweighted graphs, arbitrary fixed edge order, success probability at least two thirds and semi-streaming bit space. These choices narrow the source to one decision question about algorithm existence.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase; user-approved factor, memory allowance and stream model

context_blocks.text: A graph may contain far more edges than a small-memory algorithm can retain. One scan can reveal useful local connections, while a short path between distant vertices can depend on edges encountered in an inconvenient order. The question asks how much repeated access is needed even when only one numerical distance is requested.

The original discussion emphasizes spanners. An \((\alpha,\beta)\)-spanner is a subgraph \(H\) preserving all pairwise distances within \(d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le\alpha d_G(u,v)+\beta\). Such a summary supports many pairs, whereas this card supplies its only pair in advance. Results that exploit all-pairs summaries do not by themselves characterize the best method for that smaller output requirement.

Exact distance can be obtained with a number of passes depending on the distance. That dependence can be large on arbitrary graphs. The selected target instead demands a logarithmic worst-case pass bound and permits a controlled multiplicative error.

The SODA 2026 result gives a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation in \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}(\log n/\log\log n)^2)\) passes using \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}n\log^3 n)\) words. Fixing \(\varepsilon=1/2\) meets the accuracy and bit-space requirements here, but the number of passes is asymptotically larger than \(O(\log n)\).

The same work proves a lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)\) passes for any constant approximation in semi-streaming space, even for one fixed pair in an unweighted graph. It also explains how its communication simulation accommodates the same order in every pass. This rules out substantially fewer passes while remaining compatible with the requested logarithmic upper bound.

A positive answer would improve the known number of scans for a basic distance query without requiring the whole graph in memory. A negative answer would establish a sharper limitation on what repeated sequential access can recover, even with a constant approximation and only one requested pair.
